title: Ant, Visa, and Mastercard converge on a Know-Your-Agent framework for AI payments
subtitle: The three payment giants are bridging their proprietary agent-trust protocols — Visa TAP, Mastercard Verifiable Intent, and Ant's Agentic Mobile Protocol — through Singapore's BuildFin.ai.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Ant International, Visa, and Mastercard announced on September 10, 2026 that they are jointly developing a Know-Your-Agent (KYA) interoperability framework — the payment-side counterpart to Know-Your-Customer rules, but written for AI agents that transact on a user's behalf. The three companies each have proprietary agent-trust protocols already: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol (TAP), Mastercard's Verifiable Intent, and Ant's Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP). The new framework, coordinated through Singapore's BuildFin.ai platform (convened by the Monetary Authority of Singapore), lets an agent registered with any one of the three be recognized by the others — shared certification, common entity binding, continuous behavior monitoring.

The concrete effect for developers is that an AI agent will need one identity, not three. Today, if you are building a shopping agent that clears purchases at merchants using different card networks, you have to onboard the agent separately into each network's trust protocol, prove its provenance three times, and instrument the same behavior monitoring against three different APIs. KYA collapses that to one onboarding. The three networks project that AI agents will orchestrate $3–5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030; the framework is a bet that a common trust layer is a precondition for that number to actually happen. Without it, the fragmentation cost eats the margins.

This is also the second cross-network trust announcement in a week. On September 3 we covered Anthropic's Claude commerce agents, which shipped with Shopify, Visa, and Mastercard integrations of their own. The KYA framework is the industry's move to convert those bilateral deals into a multi-lateral standard before the pattern splinters. It follows the historical shape of payments infrastructure — bilateral rails first, then a settlement layer that lets them interoperate — but the timeline is compressed. Card networks took decades to converge on EMV; the agent-trust equivalent is being negotiated in months. That speed matters because agent commerce is scaling faster than the rulebook can be written by hand.

Takeaway for learners: agent identity is now a real engineering problem, not a policy hypothetical. If you are building anything that will act as a user in the payments system — a shopping bot, an accounts-payable agent, a subscription manager — the primitives you will be working with are being defined at BuildFin this quarter. Learn the shape of KYA (behavior scoring, revocation, cross-network attestation) the same way you would learn OAuth, because it is on the same trajectory. It will be a required skill for agent developers within eighteen months.
